pictures.scene: Juan de Juanes, The Last Supper — Christ seated at the centre of a long white-clothed table holding up a round white host in his right hand with his left laid on his breast, a green-sleeved haloed John leaning at his right and a white-bearded haloed Peter at his left, bread and a knife and a gold salt cellar set out on the cloth and a chequered floor below, at that time the disciples came to jesus and asked, who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven, jesus invited a little child to stand among them

pictures.scene: Anthony van Dyck, The Five Eldest Children of Charles I — a girl in a white silk gown with a pearl necklace standing at the left beside a smaller child in a white gown and a lace cap, a boy in red satin with a broad lace collar resting his hand on the head of a huge mastiff, a patterned red carpet underfoot and a dark green curtain hanging behind, truly i tell you, he said, unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven, therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven

pictures.scene: Ludolf Backhuysen, Storm at Sea — a small single-masted boat heeling over in a huge breaking wave with its sail bellying loose and a crowd of figures huddled together in the stern, rain slanting across a black sky with one orange break of light at the left, and whoever welcomes a little child like this in my name welcomes me, but if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea

pictures.scene: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Beggars — cripples in white smocks and fox-tail badges propped on wooden crutches and leg stumps on the green grass, one of them looking up open-mouthed and a black-cloaked figure in a wide hat walking away behind them with a bowl, a brick wall standing beyond, woe to the world for the causes of sin, these stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the man through whom they come, if your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away, it is better for you to enter life crippled or lame than to have two hands and two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire

pictures.scene: John Everett Millais, The Blind Girl — a red-haired blind girl in a brown shawl and an orange skirt with a concertina lying on her lap and a placard hung at her neck, her fair-haired sister leaning against her shoulder under a blue cloak, a double rainbow standing over a bright green meadow with cattle and a village behind them, and if your eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away, it is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the fire of hell, see that you do not look down on any of these little ones, for i tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my father in heaven

pictures.scene: Anton Mauve, The Return of the Flock — a flock of sheep seen from behind crowding up a brown heath track with a small dark-coated shepherd and his staff on the ridge above them, one white lamb standing apart at the left of the track and a pale grey sky lying across the top, what do you think, if a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost, and if he finds it, truly i tell you, he rejoices more over that one sheep than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray

pictures.scene: Gerrit Dou, Praying Old Woman — a very old woman in a dark hood and a fur-lined gown with her wrinkled hands pressed together and her eyes lowered, a clasped book lying on the table in front of her and a deep brown shadow filling the room behind, truly i tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven, again, i tell you truly that if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by my father in heaven

pictures.scene: Jan van Eyck, God Enthroned — a bearded figure crowned with a jewelled triple tiara and haloed in beaten gold with lettering running round the arch above him, a deep red mantle clasped at the breast by a great pearl and sapphire brooch and jewelled bands falling down both sides of it, jesus answered, i tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times, because of this, the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants

pictures.scene: Marinus van Reymerswaele, The Tax Collectors — a clerk in a red fur hat and a blue gown writing in a great open ledger with a quill, a second man in a green cap leaning over his shoulder and pointing down at the page while he turns a coin in his other hand, rolled documents and a brass candlestick on the shelf above them, as he began the settlements, a debtor was brought to him owing ten thousand talents, since the man was unable to pay, the master ordered that he be sold to pay his debt, along with his wife and children and everything he owned

pictures.scene: Rembrandt, The Return of the Prodigal Son — the ragged son kneeling with his shaved head against his father's breast and his worn shoes and one bare heel showing beneath him, the old father in a deep red cloak laying both hands on his shoulders with his eyes closed, a tall man in red watching from the right and two dim figures standing in the shadow behind, then the servant fell on his knees before him, have patience with me, he begged, and i will pay back everything, his master had compassion on him, forgave his debt, and released him

pictures.scene: Adriaen Brouwer, Fighting Peasants — a peasant in a blue cap and yellow breeches twisting round open-mouthed with a knife in his hand while a woman in a white headcloth throws both arms around him to hold him back, another man shouting over his shoulder and jugs and benches standing at a trestle table behind them, a village church tower on the hill beyond, but when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii, he grabbed him and began to choke him, saying, pay back what you owe me, so his fellow servant fell down and begged him, have patience with me, and i will pay you back

pictures.scene: Rembrandt, Saint Peter in Prison — the white-bearded apostle sitting alone on the floor of a stone cell in a heavy brown robe with his hands folded in his lap, the light falling across his face and over the straw at his feet where two great iron keys are lying, the rest of the cell lost in darkness, but he refused, instead, he went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt, when his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly distressed, and they went and recounted all of this to their master

pictures.scene: Nicolas Poussin, Christ and the Woman Taken in Adultery — Christ in a blue tunic and a red mantle standing in a paved square with his arm stretched out and one finger pointing down at the ground, a woman in a white shift and a blue skirt kneeling at the left with her head bowed, accusers pressing in at the right and stone houses and a long flight of steps rising behind, then the master summoned him and declared, you wicked servant, i forgave all your debt because you begged me, shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as i had on you
pictures.name: pd_poussin_christ_and_the_woman_taken_in_adultery

pictures.scene: Anthony van Dyck, Lord John Stuart and His Brother Lord Bernard Stuart — one brother standing on a stone step in a gold satin doublet and dark breeches with his elbow resting on the balustrade, the other turned away from him in a silver cloak lined with blue and blue satin breeches, looking back over his shoulder with his gloves gathered in his hand, pale boots on them both and a bare stone wall behind, in anger his master turned him over to the jailers to be tortured, until he should repay all that he owed, that is how my heavenly father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart
pictures.name: pd_van_dyck_stuart_brothers

lines.text: At that time the disciples came to Jesus and asked, Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?
Jesus invited a little child to stand among them.
Truly I tell you, He said, unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
And whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me.
But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea.
Woe to the world for the causes of sin. These stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the man through whom they come!
If your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life crippled or lame than to have two hands and two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire.
And if your eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the fire of hell.
See that you do not look down on any of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father in heaven.
What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost?
And if he finds it, truly I tell you, he rejoices more over that one sheep than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray.
In the same way, your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.
If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over.
But if he will not listen, take one or two others along, so that every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector.
Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.
Again, I tell you truly that if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven.
For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them.
Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother who sins against me? Up to seven times?
Jesus answered, I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!
Because of this, the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants.
As he began the settlements, a debtor was brought to him owing ten thousand talents.
Since the man was unable to pay, the master ordered that he be sold to pay his debt, along with his wife and children and everything he owned.
Then the servant fell on his knees before him. Have patience with me, he begged, and I will pay back everything.
His master had compassion on him, forgave his debt, and released him.
But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. He grabbed him and began to choke him, saying, Pay back what you owe me!
So his fellow servant fell down and begged him, Have patience with me, and I will pay you back.
But he refused. Instead, he went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt.
When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly distressed, and they went and recounted all of this to their master.
Then the master summoned him and declared, You wicked servant! I forgave all your debt because you begged me.
Shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?
In anger his master turned him over to the jailers to be tortured, until he should repay all that he owed.
That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.
